lesson.title: Trading Places: One Element Displaces Another
lesson.summary: A single replacement reaction occurs when a free element takes the place of a different element inside a compound, following the pattern A plus BC forms AC plus B.
lesson.body:
Single replacement reactions round out the trio of specific reaction patterns branching off Reaction Types Overview, alongside synthesis and decomposition. The pattern here is different from both of those: instead of combining substances or breaking one apart, a single replacement reaction has one free, uncombined element step in and take the place of a different element that was already bonded inside a compound, following the general form A + BC -> AC + B. The element that was displaced is left over on its own, now free and uncombined, just as the element that did the displacing started out.

Whether this kind of swap actually happens depends on relative reactivity: some elements are more prone to giving up electrons and forming new bonds than others, and a more reactive element can displace a less reactive one from a compound, while the reverse generally will not happen on its own. You will see this reactivity ranking formalized later as an activity series, but the core idea to hold onto now is simple: displacement is not automatic, it happens specifically because one element is more chemically eager to react than the one it replaces.

A classic laboratory example is the reaction between zinc metal and hydrochloric acid: Zn(s) + 2 HCl(aq) -> ZnCl2(aq) + H2(g). Zinc, a reactive metal, displaces the hydrogen that was bonded to chlorine in hydrochloric acid. The zinc ends up bonded to the chloride ions instead, forming dissolved zinc chloride, while the displaced hydrogen is left over as free H2 gas, which you can literally watch bubble up out of the solution as the reaction proceeds, a direct visual payoff of the (g) state symbol introduced back in State Symbols.

Check the balance atom by atom. The left side has 1 zinc atom from Zn, and 2 HCl contributes 2 hydrogen atoms and 2 chlorine atoms. The right side has ZnCl2, contributing 1 zinc atom and 2 chlorine atoms, plus H2, contributing 2 hydrogen atoms. Both sides show 1 Zn, 2 H, and 2 Cl, so the equation is balanced. It is also worth reading the coefficients here the way you learned in Coefficients: the 2 in front of HCl is a mole ratio, saying that exactly two moles of hydrochloric acid are needed for every one mole of zinc that reacts, not an arbitrary number tacked on to make the equation look right.

With synthesis, decomposition, and single replacement now covered in detail, you have direct experience with three of the five reaction families sketched out in the overview chapter. Double replacement and combustion were introduced there conceptually, through the silver chloride precipitation and propane combustion examples, and the same balancing, coefficient, and state-symbol tools you have built across this unit apply to every one of them.
